svg.title: Two ways to stop per-VLAN PIM explosion: MVR replicates one multicast VLAN into user VLANs, PIM snooping prunes router ports on a shared segment
svg.desc: Left: the problem - a source in VLAN 100 and users in VLAN 200, 300 and 400, which the traditional answer solves by configuring PIM in every VLAN. Middle: MVR moves the stream once into a multicast VLAN and replicates it into the user VLANs, translating each user's IGMP join into a subscription on the multicast VLAN; one configuration instead of four, but receive-only and heavily vendor dependent. Right: PIM snooping solves a different problem - ten routers sharing one Layer 2 segment exchange PIM hellos, and without snooping every router receives every stream; with snooping the switch only forwards to ports where a PIM neighbour actually joined. A bottom band gives the selection rule: MVR for many user VLANs with receive-only IPTV, PIM snooping for many routers on a shared segment, and neither for a routed access layer.
svg.text: Two Layer 2 aggregation problems, two features
MVR is about too many user VLANs. PIM snooping is about too many routers on one segment. They are not alternatives.
Traditional answer: PIM in every VLAN.
Four configurations, four chances to differ.

Neither. One router per VLAN, no shared
Both features move the problem rather than solving it: the real question is why many VLANs or many routers share one broadcast domain.
If the answer is "history", the design debt is in the addressing plan, not in the switch configuration.
Test on the model, not on the datasheet
MVR and PIM snooping are the two features where vendor documents promise more than the code does. Channel-change time and per-port group limits must be measured on the exact hardware in the LLD.
